Nov 4 : Chinese genetic sequencing firm Novogene sued the Pentagon late Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Washington over its inclusion on a US list of companies allegedly aiding Beijing's military. In June, the Defense Department added Novogene, Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba internet search provider Baidu and automakers BYD and NIO and others to its list of "Chinese military companies" that prohibits the Defense Department from contracting directly with the firms. A number of Chinese firms have sued the Pentagon over the designations.

IRAN: Iran's government savoured the stinging rebuke delivered to Donald Trump in the midterm elections, declaring voters had rejected the war launched by the US president even as Tehran remained on high alert for the possibility of renewed strikes. "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Iran's chief negotiator, posted on X on Wednesday (Nov 4), adding that Washington should not ignore public opinion by attacking his country again. Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a written statement that US hostility would persist regardless of which party was in power, warning against "even the slightest inclination towards submission" to the US . "The US sees the end of its hegemony as distant; we see it as near," he added. OLD FOES

Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and Ho us e in Tuesday's election , with victories in Republican strongholds underscoring deep fr us tration with Trump 's stewardship of the economy and his decision to launch a war that drove up gas prices. In Iran, a news outlet run by the judiciary shared a joke circulating on X that " Trump failed at regime change in Iran but he succeeded in Texas", a reference to the southern state where a Democrat won a Senate race for the first time in decades. But two senior Iranian sources told Reuters that while Iranian leaders welcomed the Democrats’ victory, Tehran was concerned that Trump could seek to compensate for it with a military strike, and remained on high alert. Iran's leaders have long regarded the United States as their main enemy, referring to it as "the Great Satan". At a state-organised rally on Wednesday commemorating the student takeover of the US embassy in Tehran during the 1979 Islamic revolution, demonstrators voiced triumph at an election they linked to Iran's success in surviving months of US attacks. "The fact that the might of these warmongering Republicans has been broken, something unprecedented in human history, means that from now on we will see the real war unfolding inside the US Senate and among American officials ," said one, giving only his family name of Nazari.

Pictures of US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on a dartboard during the 47th anniversary of the US expulsion from Iran, in Tehran, Nov 4, 2026. (Photo: West Asia News Agency via REUTERS/Majid Asgaripour)

Mediators have intensified efforts to end the war amid fears it could reignite after the election , with Trump on Tuesday declining to rule out a resumption of combat operations after the vote and Iran planning wider retaliation if war resumes. The US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb 28, and Iran responded with strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. Conflict also erupted in Lebanon between Iran-backed Hezbollah and Israel, and more recently spread to Yemen, from where the Iran-aligned Houthis have struck energy facilities, airports and other targets in Saudi Arabia. Global oil and gas prices have shot up with shipping through the Strait of Hormuz severely disrupted after Tehran declared it closed, while the US has imposed a naval blockade on Iran, hitting Iran's economy hard. "IRAN'S SHADOW OVER US ELECTIONS" Ahead of the US election, senior Iranian officials told Reuters that Tehran was deliberately prolonging talks with the US to weaken Trump politically ahead of the vote. Some news outlets played on the timing of the election on the anniversary of the embassy seizure, when radical students cemented Iran's toppling of the US -backed Shah by storming the embassy and holding 52 Americans hostage there for 444 days. Major Iranian newspaper Hamshahri linked the events with a front-page image showing Trump blindfolded with his head bowed. With a headline declaring "Iran's shadow over US elections", it said Washington had been "47 years Iran's captive: from the capture of the spies' nest ( US embassy) to the November 2026 US Congress elections". The Iran war has been unpopular among Americans since it began, and blaming the war for driving up costs was a foc us of the Democrats' election campaign. Khamenei's message signalled that Tehran had no intention of showing flexibility on its demands for lasting control over the Strait of Hormuz or conditions to end the conflict. "The consequences of ( US ) miscalculations and arrogant del us ions have manifested as a heavy burden of costs, borne by the American people and the puppet regimes subservient to the US government," he said. Trump has offered shifting goals and timelines for the war that is now in its ninth month. "I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," Trump told Fox News, referring to the election result. The conservative Iranian newspaper Jam-e Jam declared the election result "The twilight of Trump ism".

BRUGES, Belgium, Nov 4 : Hackers who cranked up fridge temperatures at supermarkets across Europe may have gained access through public internet-connected systems protected by default passwords or outdated software, a cybersecurity expert said. The second cyberattack in three weeks hit fridge systems at supermarket chains including Carrefour and Delhaize in Belgium, and ICA and Coop in Sweden, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food and raising concerns about food security. Three blood banks in France were also hit. Authorities have not publicly disclosed how the attackers gained access, and no perpetrator has been identified. Laurens Singier, an ethical hacker and researcher at Cyber 3 Lab, part of Howest University of Applied Sciences in Bruges, Belgium, said internet-connected systems which can be accessible remotely often have weak protections.

"In this case, the weak point was mainly putting those devices on the public internet. They shouldn't even be there," he said, speaking from a lab full of servers and systems similar to those that could control supermarket store fridges. A common problem with such systems is that operators fail to change default passwords set by the manufacturer, while others run older software with known vulnerabilities, he said. AI was now making it easier for amateurs to pull off hacks, Singier added. Supermarkets on Tuesday said they had taken hacked fridges offline, in line with guidance from refrigeration monitoring software provider Danfoss, whose systems were again among those targeted. Danfoss has said it is working with clients on fixes. Singier said that retailers should check they understand how they connect to the store interface, strengthen passwords, and consider switching from internet-based systems to more secure systems using SIM cards, like those used by solar panels and car chargers. "After this attack, we've seen a lot less of these devices publicly on the internet," he said. "But if you look at the numbers, there's still a lot of industrial devices which are open to the public, and in a lot of cases you yourself as the butcher or the chocolatier don't even know about it."

Source: Reuters

PARIS, Nov 4 : World number one Alexander Zverev's reign at the top of the rankings got off to a disappointing start on Wednesday as Italy's Lorenzo Musetti upset the German top seed 7-6(5) 6-2 in the Paris Masters round of 32. The 29-year-old, who climbed to number one on Monday, suffered surprise defeat days after losing to Australia's Alex de Minaur in the Vienna Open semi-finals. Musetti, a former world number five, seized the initiative by winning six of the final seven points of the opening-set tiebreak before taking command of the second set. The 24-year-old Italian broke Zverev for a 2-1 lead and struck again to move 5-2 ahead on his way to victory.

World number 24 Musetti, a former French Open and Wimbledon semi-finalist, fired 29 winners and eight aces during the one-hour, 40-mnute contest to improve his head-to-head record against Zverev to 4-2. "It's pretty shocking the level I was able to play in front of Sascha, who was serving really well, especially in the first set," Musetti said. "It was really close. It could have gone both ways." The win continued a resurgence for Musetti, who has been hampered by injuries throughout the 2026 season. His toughest setback came at the Australian Open, where he retired while leading 24-times Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic by two sets in their quarter-final. Musetti ended a four-year wait for a title in Lyon last month. Zverev has enjoyed a breakthrough season, capturing his maiden Grand Slam title at the French Open before adding a second major crown at the US Open. He has secured his place at the season-ending ATP Finals in Turin this month.

WASHINGTON, Nov 4 : Prediction markets got the big picture right in the US midterm elections, although a few races delivered surprises as Democrats seized control of the Senate and House of Representatives. With more than $1.48 billion wagered on Tuesday's elections, the results offered a test of whether prediction markets could translate their odds into accurate electoral forecasts. Bets placed on a Democratic midterm sweep largely paid off despite some mispriced races, as tens of millions of voters delivered a stinging rebuke to US President Donald Trump. "Prediction markets priced the midterm outcome within hours," said Kelly Ye, head of research at digital asset trading platform Talos.

Several closely contested Senate races had attracted millions of dollars in bets, putting prediction markets under scrutiny. In many cases, the results tracked expectations, with Democrats winning Senate seats in Texas and Ohio. "This was the first true prediction markets election," said Harry Crane, professor of statistics at Rutgers University. "The markets projected Democratic wins across the board throughout the closing weeks of the campaign, and were quick to react in real time to voting information as it rolled in," he added. Prediction markets rose to prominence as they diverged from traditional opinion polls by signaling a Trump victory in 2024, and analysts were scrutinizing their performance this week. While the markets cite high accuracy rates in their betting odds, some high-profile misses during the US primaries and in Brazil's presidential election have shown they are fallible. Prediction markets allow users to buy and sell contracts tied to real-world events, with prices reflecting traders' collective expectations. Critics, however, say those odds can be skewed by speculation, thin liquidity and concentrated bets. Kalshi's total trading volume on election markets reached over $2.5 billion this cycle, compared with $1.3 billion during the 2024 election cycle, which included the presidential race. Traders on Kalshi were assigning a 55 per cent probability to a "blue tsunami" as early as April. Meanwhile, Polymarket's election forecasts were about 98 per cent accurate, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. One notable miss came in conservative South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Darline Graham to win a Senate seat, defying market expectations. Kalshi and Polymarket had implied a 70 per cent chance of Graham, the sister of the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, winning that race as of late afternoon Tuesday. "Prediction markets can be useful because they aggregate the views of people who have an incentive to be right, not just to express an opinion," said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. "They can give a good indication of where the weight of information is pointing, but a prediction isn't a promise. Whether it’s politics or sports, you still have to hold the election or play the game to know the result," he added.

Source: Reuters

Nov 4 : The International Ice Hockey Federation said on Wednesday it maintains its disagreement with a Court of Arbitration for Sport decision to reinstate Russian teams, warning of "significant practical and sporting challenges". The statement follows announcements from Norway, Denmark, Sweden and the Czech Republic that their national teams will refuse to play against Russia at next year's men's World Championships in Germany. Nov 4 : Qualcomm has signed a multi-year agreement with SpaceX to supply radio equipment, baseband units and software for Starlink Mobile's planned nationwide terrestrial 5G network, as the Elon Musk-led space company seeks to challenge established US wireless carriers. The equipment will be deployed across tens of thousands of macro cell sites in the country starting in 2027, Qualcomm said on Wednesday. While the company did not disclose the financial terms of the agreement, it said "this is our biggest 5G deal yet." The deal will expand the presence of Qualcomm, best known for the chips that power smartphones, in the telecom infrastructure market, where it will compete with Marvell, Broadcom and Intel by supplying chips used in cell tower gear. Qualcomm, which has been seeking to diversify beyond mobile devices, already helps power 5G networks in Japan and Vietnam.

FAST

Nov 4 : The rise of AI-led shopping is posing a conundrum for retailers like Walmart and Amazon: how to enable AI agents to shop on their websites, without threatening their lucrative advertising revenue and the customer data that fuels it. Retail powerhouses Walmart and Amazon are also the world's two largest retail media businesses, dominating the estimated $74.4 billion in US retail media spending with a combined 88 per cent share of that market, according to projections from data firm Emarketer. But digital assistants could soon disrupt that business. AI-powered agents that can research and purchase products on consumers' behalf — like Meta's recently released Muse — could erode the highly profitable business of brands paying retailers to promote products on their websites and apps. Morgan Stanley researchers said in July these agents could account for 10 per cent to 20 per cent of US e-commerce spending by 2030. Amazon and Walmart are taking different approaches to agentic AI shopping. Amazon has blocked Muse, while Walmart is officially partnering with Meta's agentic tool.

So far, there is no meaningful effect yet on Amazon ads from third-party agents, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said last week. However, the company's 11 per cent year-over-year growth in advertising revenue for the third quarter was its slowest pace of growth in nearly four years, LSEG data show. The segment consistently accounts for about 10 per cent of total net sales. DIFFERENT APPROACHES Amazon banned Muse from its website in September, saying it appeared to have accessed its online store without authorization, capturing and storing customer credentials. Meta declined to comment. The e-commerce leader told Reuters this week that third-party agents should operate openly and respect service providers' decisions about whether or not to participate. Amazon also won a court order blocking Perplexity's shopping agent Comet in March, though the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals overturned the ban in August, a decision Amazon said it disagreed with. The case is ongoing. Walmart, conversely, rolled out infrastructure on October 21 to enable third-party agentic commerce. When a shopper uses an agent to browse, Walmart will create a profile for that agent that links to the shopper's Walmart account. Consumers can approve purchases or set spending limits. Walmart CFO John David Rainey told analysts and investors in August that advertising, which includes the Walmart Connect retail media business, along with its membership and marketplace operations, accounted for 45 per cent of quarterly operating income growth. Walmart does not separately break out Walmart Connect's figures in its earnings release. Dan Marc, CEO of retail media platform Footprints AI, said he expects companies like Amazon and Walmart to start signing their largest advertisers to multiyear ad deals to secure those revenues, and also expects more discounts on digital retail media ads as shoppers turn to large language models and agentic tools. Walmart declined to comment. SHIFTING MARKETING LANDSCAPE Morningstar analyst Brett Husslein said the moment presents "an evolution rather than an existential threat" for retail media. Brands are expected to spend 22.6 per cent more on retail media in 2026 than last year's $60.7 billion, Emarketer forecasts show. This year, Walmart started testing ads within Sparky, its AI shopping chatbot, just as Amazon has embedded them in its AI shopping assistant, Alexa for Shopping. Advertising for bots may rely less on visual flair or emotional resonance and more on specific product data that matches customer queries using AI chatbots, industry practitioners and consultants say. Companies including Procter & Gamble, Nestle and L'Oreal have said they are trying to make product information digestible for AI agents. Those agents are bringing brands closer to consumers, said Mondelez's vice president of global digital commerce, Andrew Lederman, on a podcast in April. He said retailer media sites currently still drive the vast majority of volume for the company. "We are not recommending that clients fundamentally shift their retail media budgets overnight," said Amie Owen, chief client officer at digital commerce consultancy Flywheel. "But we are advising them to prepare for how discovery and purchase decisions may evolve." Katherine Black, a senior consultant at Kearney, envisions a radical shift, in which retail media eventually evolves into a kind of "bidding system" where agents search for a product at a consumer’s price point, and retailers set price ceilings and floors. "All retailers need to be thinking about how to interact with consumers in new ways," Black said.

Source: Reuters

MADRID, Nov 4 : Real Madrid are set to add a champion from another sporting arena to their boardroom, with 22-times tennis Grand Slam winner Rafael Nadal's appointment as a director to be put to members for ratification, the club said on Wednesday. The board agreed at its November 4 meeting to submit the appointment to the General Assembly of Delegated Members. Nadal is already an honorary member of the club. "It is a source of immense pride for Real Madrid and for all our supporters that a figure of his sporting and personal stature ... is to join our Board of Directors," Real said in a statement. The club highlighted Nadal's sporting achievements, including 92 tour singles titles, two Olympic gold medals, five Davis Cup triumphs with Spain and the world number one ranking.

Real said his qualities beyond those honours — including humility, respect for opponents and commitment to charity — also reflected the club's identity. "All these values form part of Real Madrid's identity, and Rafael Nadal has embodied and championed them throughout his sporting career," the statement said. Nadal welcomed the invitation. "I would like to thank President Florentino Perez and the Board for inviting me to join the Board of Directors of Real Madrid," he wrote on social media. "I have accepted this invitation with great enthusiasm, keen to learn and to contribute as much as I can." Nadal, who retired from tennis in November 2024, has long been touted as a potential successor to Real president Florentino Perez, although he has played down the prospect. Perez, 79, secured another four-year term in June after Real's first contested presidential election in two decades. More than a third of voting members backed challenger Enrique Riquelme, who opposed plans to bring outside investment into the member-owned club.

Source: Reuters
